source.title: Compositional Concept-Based Neuron-Level Interpretability for Deep Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Ze-Yu Jiang; Hai Huang; Xingquan Zuo

record.tranche_reason: Extends neuron-level explanation analysis to deep reinforcement-learning agents and reports neuron-concept alignment and targeted perturbation outcomes, but does not test the listed language-model claims directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports neuron-concept similarity scores, architecture-sweep trends, and selected perturbation examples. The perturbation examples are not a systematic held-out evaluation of where explanations predict neuron firing. No listed version's specific claim is directly tested. The text's reported near-optimal task performance and the Figure 2 architecture trend are not results about the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a compositional-concept method for explaining neurons in small DQN agents (Blackjack, LunarLander). It does not cite or test any version. It reports no share of interpretable neurons, no language or vision models, no InceptionV1 analysis, no attribution graphs, and no held-out simulation scoring. The width/depth sweep measures mean Jaccard alignment in 64–512-unit MLPs. That is a related construct, not V4's share of interpretable neurons under better tools or modern architectures. No enum value fits exactly: the paper neither cites nor discusses the claim, so 'discusses' is used loosely.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim the perturbation validation confirms the explanations are causal, not correlational. They also report that larger networks show lower neuron–concept alignment, which is why they chose the 64×3 network.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses value-sensitive discretization, logical concept composition, and Jaccard matching in DRL; it does not use the Qwen neuron-pole audit or the cited language-model explanation methods as its evaluation recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Mean Jaccard similarity decreases monotonically with network width; depth 3 achieves optimal alignment among the tested depths. The paper does not state numeric scores for these architecture comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected DQN penultimate-layer neurons match compositional logical formulas with Jaccard 0.60–0.999, scored on the analysis set used to find them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small DRL agents, selected neurons align with compositional state-feature formulas.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean neuron–concept Jaccard decreases with width (64 to 512) and peaks at depth 3; all configurations solve the task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small DRL MLPs, wider networks show lower neuron–concept alignment at similar reward.

fits_no_version.finding: In four selected cases, perturbing the state features named by a neuron's formula deactivated the neuron and changed the chosen action.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For selected DRL neurons, violating the explaining concept flips activation and action.

record.problems: Neuron matching scores are computed on the neuron-analysis states used to derive explanations; no held-out activation evaluation is stated. Causal validation consists of selected examples, with no reported aggregate or uncertainty estimates. Figure 2 gives architecture trends without numeric values in the text.

untested.parts: All: other language models, dense or MoE, and scale.
All: the InceptionV1 cat/car neuron and recursive generalization.
Share of interpretable neurons as tools improve or under modern architectures, and the vision-model estimates. The paper reports only mean Jaccard versus MLP width/depth in DRL.
All: neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models.
Held-out prediction of firing from activating-example explanations. The paper gives only selected perturbation cases.

record.verdict_notes: This is a DRL method paper with no connection to the originals. It analyses only neurons active in at least 5% of states and reports no fraction of neurons explained. The relation enum lacks an exact fit for a paper that neither tests nor cites the claim; this is T6.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares and the proportions of one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood poles.
Shares across language models, dense or mixture-of-experts architectures, and models up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.

The share of interpretable neurons, tool quality, modern language or vision architectures, and the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates. The paper reports DRL architecture trends in mean Jaccard similarity, a related but different measure.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction without a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations fitted on activating examples fail to predict firing on held-out activations. The paper reports selected state-perturbation examples, not that evaluation.
Automated scoring of explanations on new text and the share of neurons attaining good scores.

rows.subject: DQN LunarLander-v3
rows.size_stated: three fully connected layers (64 units each)
rows.operation_detail: Matched neuron activation patterns to compositional concepts using Jaccard similarity.
rows.measure: Neuron-concept Jaccard similarity; the best formula is LLeg ∧ RLeg.
rows.note: The authors describe the neuron as a ground-contact detector. Similarity is measured on the neuron-analysis states used to find the explanation, not on a stated held-out activation set.
rows.check: Hand-picked showcase neuron, not a population share. The Jaccard score is computed on the same 10,000-state analysis set used to search for the formula. The same applies to r2–r8.
